claims.claim: Biomedical ethics examines moral questions arising in medicine, healthcare, and the life sciences, including patient autonomy, access to and distribution of medical resources, human experimentation, and life-and-death decisions; the term bioethics was coined in 1970 by the American biochemist Van Rensselaer Potter.

The four-principles framework of biomedical ethics — respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, and justice — was developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress; the principles are prima facie, mid-level considerations to be specified and balanced in context, so the framework is not a formula that settles cases automatically.

Informed consent requires that a person with decision-making capacity consent voluntarily, on the basis of adequate information and understanding; it functions as an ethical legitimacy requirement for medical intervention and research and is reflected in human-rights documents and law, with legal details varying by jurisdiction.

End-of-life ethics commonly distinguishes killing a patient from allowing a patient to die, where allowing to die includes withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment; the moral significance of this distinction is contested, for example by arguments that intent and outcome are the same in paradigm cases.

Advance directives — such as living wills and the designation of a surrogate decision-maker — let people record wishes for future care; whether and how earlier directives should bind later decisions is philosophically contested and context-dependent, with substituted-judgment and best-interests standards offering different bases for decision-making.

Justice in healthcare concerns fair access to care and the fair allocation of scarce resources; when needs cannot all be met, rationing questions arise on which reasonable people disagree, and fair-process approaches such as accountability for reasonableness have been proposed for making such decisions.
Ethical analysis of healthcare questions clarifies concepts, values, and arguments in general terms and is distinct from individualized clinical or legal advice for a particular person's situation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Moral significance of the killing-versus-allowing-to-die distinction
positions: Withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment is morally different from actively ending a life, so allowing to die can be permissible where killing is not.
In paradigm cases the intent and the outcome are the same, so the acting-versus-omitting distinction cannot bear the moral weight alone (Rachels-style argument).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as an open philosophical dispute in the lesson; neither position endorsed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Authority of advance directives over later decisions
positions: Earlier expressed wishes should be honored as the patient's own precedent autonomy (substituted judgment).
The later self may differ in interests or identity, so the best-interests standard should govern.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as contested and context-dependent; the lesson describes both standards without endorsing either.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Criteria for allocating scarce healthcare resources
positions: Priority should go to those worst off in health.
Priority should go to interventions producing the greatest aggregate benefit.
Because reasonable people disagree, decisions should be made through a fair, revisable, publicly justified process.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All positions presented neutrally; the lesson notes reasonable disagreement and fair-process proposals without endorsing a criterion.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Autonomy versus beneficence in treatment decisions
positions: Respect for autonomy generally requires honoring a capacitated patient's informed, voluntary refusal.
Beneficence supports caregivers acting for what they judge to be the patient's good.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a conflict the framework asks practitioners and students to weigh openly in context.

sourceRecords.title: 10.1 The Challenge of Bioethics — Introduction to Philosophy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the scope of bioethics (patient autonomy, distribution of and access to medical resources, human experimentation, life-and-death decisions), the 1970 coinage of the term bioethics by Van Rensselaer Potter, the active/passive and voluntary/nonvoluntary distinctions in euthanasia, living wills and DNR orders as advance directives, the opportunity-cost framing of allocation, and Rachels' challenge to the active/passive distinction. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Informed Consent
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports informed consent as informed, voluntary, decisionally-capacitated consent (information, comprehension, voluntariness), its role as a legitimacy requirement for medical intervention, its reflection in human-rights documents and law (with jurisdiction-specific details), its grounding in respect for autonomy and its conflicts with beneficence, and the Beauchamp-and-Childress autonomy framing. Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Advance Directives
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the definitions of advance directive, living will, and surrogate designation; the substituted-judgment and best-interests standards; and the contested philosophical questions about honoring earlier directives (autonomy over time, personal identity, precedent autonomy). Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Justice and Access to Health Care
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports distributive justice in healthcare: value judgments embedded in defining equal access, reasonable disagreement about tradeoffs, 'unsolved rationing problems' (Daniels), and fair-process approaches such as accountability for reasonableness (Daniels and Sabin). Reference only; original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Bioethics
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports the four-principle approach (principlism) developed by Tom Beauchamp and James Childress — autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice — as universal prima facie mid-level principles, the common-morality framing, and the methods of specification and balancing. Reference only; original prose.
